corrected_what_is_reported: Scroll reported that its analysis found 200 booths across 58 constituencies in 26 Bihar districts where between 324 and 641 names were deleted from the draft roll, 77,454 in all. It reported that most deleted voters its team met in 10 of those booths had been marked absent or shifted though they had lived at their addresses for years, and that interviews with 17 BLOs showed no consistent procedure for deciding deletions.
corrected_figures: 200 booths, 58 constituencies, 26 districts; 324 to 641 deletions per booth; 77,454 deleted across the 200 booths; 10 booths visited; 100 people interviewed; 17 BLOs interviewed
official_response: Parth Gupta, electoral registration officer for Purnia, acknowledged that Jhurana Das should not have been asked for her parents' documents: “Please provide her details and I will look into it.” Scroll also reported that Election Commission spokespersons and Bihar Chief Electoral Officer Vinod Singh Gunjiyal did not respond to requests for comment.
evidence: Our analysis revealed that 200 booths across 58 constituencies in 26 districts recorded unusually high deletions – the names of between 324 to 641 voters were deleted in these booths.
In total, 77,454 voters were deleted across the 200 booths.
Our team visited 10 among the 200 booths in three constituencies – Purnia, Hajipur, and Digha – and interviewed 100 people
Most voters we met had been marked either “absent,” or “shifted,” even though they had been residing at their addresses for many years.
Our interviews with 17 BLOs – three in person and 14 over the phone – across nine constituencies ... showed that there was no consistency in the process they followed to delete voters.

Parth Gupta, the electoral registration officer for Purnia, who is overseeing the booth, acknowledged that Jhurana should not have been asked to furnish these documents. “Please provide her details and I will look into it,” he said.
Election Commission spokespersons and Vinod Singh Gunjiyal, Bihar’s Chief Electoral Officer, did not respond to requests for comment.

corrected_what_is_reported: Newslaundry reported that several voters in Delhi's Okhla constituency whose names were removed before the SIR began said they got no notice or hearing and learnt of the deletion only when they tried to take part in the SIR. It reported that 34,644 names were deleted in Okhla during the 2026 mapping phase, against 9,170 in all of 2025.
corrected_figures: Okhla deletions 9,170 in 2025 and 34,644 in the 2026 mapping phase; Delhi about 1.55 crore voters last year, about 1.45 crore when SIR began; more than 47 lakh excluded from the draft of August 31; about 33 lakh notices; more than 10 lakh net deletions before SIR
official_response: Delhi Chief Electoral Officer Ashok Kumar said that no voter had been deleted without an inquiry and an opportunity for a hearing.
evidence: Yet several voters whose names disappeared before the exercise told Newslaundry that they were not informed about their deletion and did not get an opportunity to contest it.
In Okhla alone, 9,170 names were deleted in 2025. But in 2026, during the mapping phase, a further 34,644 additional names were deleted – nearly 4 times as many in roughly half the time.
As questions emerged about the pre-SIR deletions, Delhi Chief Electoral Officer Ashok Kumar said that no voter had been deleted without an inquiry and an opportunity for a hearing.
But the voters Newslaundry spoke to said they did not know their names had been removed until they attempted to participate in the SIR process.
Last year, Delhi had around 1.55 crore registered voters. By the time the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise began this year, that number had already fallen to around 1.45 crore.
more than 10 lakh net deletions took place between the 2025 Delhi assembly elections and before the SIR exercise officially began.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported the deaths of two BLOs. The family of Aneesh George in Kannur, Kerala, alleged he was under pressure to finish by December 4, and police said a note found on Mukesh Jangid in Jaipur said he faced extreme pressure from his supervisor and was told he would be suspended if he did not meet his SIR target. It also reported that revenue employees in Tamil Nadu announced a statewide boycott of SIR work over workload.
corrected_figures: 1,065 enumeration forms issued to George, 50 left to distribute on November 16; George aged 44; Jangid aged 45
official_response: Kannur District Collector Arun K Vijayan's report indicated that the BLO was not under any work pressure. The Indian Express said its multiple calls and messages to Rajasthan CEO Naveen got no response.
evidence: George, 44, the BLO for booth number 18 under Payyanur Assembly seat in Kannur district, was found dead in his house. No suicide note was recovered but his family and close friends alleged that George ... was under pressure to complete his job within the stipulated time, that is, by December 4.

Bindayaka police station in-charge Vinod Kumar told The Indian Express: “A suicide note was recovered from his body which stated that he was facing extreme work pressure from his supervisor. He was asked to complete his target of the SIR process or he will be suspended. He stated in the note that he wasn’t able to sleep at night for the last few days.”
In Tamil Nadu, the Federation of Associations of Revenue Employees (FERA) said it will begin a statewide boycott of the SIR exercise from November 18

Kannur District Collector Arun K Vijayan ... indicated that the BLO was not under any work pressure. The collector said 1,065 enumeration forms had been issued to George for distribution. Upon verification on November 16, it was found that only 50 forms remained to be distributed.
The Indian Express made multiple calls and sent messages to state CEO Naveen but did not receive any response.
problem: Minor wording only. The note, as quoted by police, says he was asked to complete his target or be suspended. It does not explicitly say the supervisor issued the threat, so the summary was tightened.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that two women assistant BLOs died of heart attacks in Tapi and Vadodara districts, bringing BLO deaths in Gujarat that week to four. The husband of one, Usha Solanki, said she was a heart patient who had asked to be excused from BLO duty, which the Vadodara Collector disputed.
corrected_figures: four BLO deaths in Gujarat in a week; Kalpanaben Patel aged 56; Usha Solanki aged 50
official_response: Vadodara District Collector Anil Dhameliya: “We checked with the institute as well as with the local officials. She had not made any official request to be excused (from BLO duty)… We have learnt now that she was suffering from a heart ailment and had episodes of fainting in her institute as well.” He also said: “We have been cautious about ensuring that there is no excessive workload on the BLOs and therefore, we have appointed additional staff to assist in the process.” An unnamed government official: “With a large workforce of over two lakh involved in the SIR work, these deaths can be termed as natural. Linking these to SIR is not justified and logical.”
evidence: TWO WOMAN assistant Booth Level Officers (BLOs) died of heart attack in Gujarat

With the two cases, the number of deaths of BLOs in Gujarat this week rose to four. A BLO from Kheda reportedly died of heart attack on Thursday and another BLO allegedly died by suicide in Gir Somnath district on Friday.

Solanki’s husband Indrasinh said she was a heart patient and had requested to be excused from BLO duty. However, the Vadodara District Collector said that no formal request was made by the assistant BLO or her family to excuse her from the exercise.
Dhameliya said that there is no excessive workload on the BLOs and many had also been relieved at request.
“We have been cautious about ensuring that there is no excessive workload on the BLOs and therefore, we have appointed additional staff to assist in the process…”
“With a large workforce of over two lakh involved in the SIR work, these deaths can be termed as natural. Linking these to SIR is not justified and logical.”
problem: The official response put "there is no excessive workload on the BLOs" in quotation marks as if Dhameliya said it verbatim. The article gives that line as paraphrase. His direct quote is the longer sentence about being cautious to ensure no excessive workload. The Collector's statement that she had a heart ailment and fainting episodes was also omitted.

corrected_what_is_reported: The BBC reported that 10 BLOs it spoke to in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal said they worked 14 to 15 hours a day with little rest, and that families linked the deaths of more than a dozen poll workers, by alleged suicide or heart attack, to election work stress. The BBC said it had not independently verified the causes of death. It reported BLOs saying the SIR app crashed often and that many had not been paid.
corrected_figures: 10 BLOs interviewed; 14 to 15 hours a day; more than a dozen workers died; BLO pay doubled from 6,000 to 12,000 rupees; supervisors' pay raised from 12,000 to 18,000 rupees
official_response: The EC has not responded to a detailed list of questions from the BBC. Media reports quoting a court affidavit say the EC has denied opposition claims linking BLO deaths to SIR work, calling them "false, exaggerated and politically motivated".
evidence: The BBC spoke to 10 BLOs in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal ... They said they were working 14–15 hours a day with little rest, minimal sleep, and meagre pay.

The punishing schedules have sparked outrage, especially after more than a dozen workers, including Kumar, died. Families have linked the deaths - from alleged suicides or heart attacks - to election work-related stress. The BBC has not independently verified the causes of death.
Many BLOs told the BBC that the government app to upload SIR forms crashed often
But many BLOs told the BBC they hadn't received any payment, and some didn't even know how much they were owed.
The EC now has doubled BLO pay from 6,000 ($66; £50) to 12,000 rupees
The EC has not responded to a detailed list of questions from the BBC.
Media reports quoting a court affidavit say the EC has denied opposition claims linking BLO deaths to SIR work, calling them "false, exaggerated and politically motivated".

corrected_what_is_reported: The Hindu reported that the Supreme Court agreed to consider an application by Congress MP Tanuj Punia alleging that Form 7 objections in the Uttar Pradesh SIR were filed with false particulars, forged signatures and in the names of people who later denied filing them. The application cited one person filing objections against 32 electors in Hata, Kushinagar, and a UP Congress claim of 700 to 800 objections in four Khalilabad booths.
corrected_figures: 32 electors objected to by one person in Hata, Kushinagar; 700-800 Form 7 objections in booths 71 to 74 of Khalilabad, as claimed by the UP Congress president
evidence: The Supreme Court has agreed to consider a plea by Congress MP Tanuj Punia highlighting widespread misuse and fraud in connection with Form 7

Mr. Punia’s application said there were credible reports indicating that “numerous” Form-7 applications were generated and submitted with incomplete or false particulars of the objector, invalid identifying details, forged signatures, and, in several instances, in the names of persons who had subsequently denied filing any such objections.

The application referred specifically to one instance in which a person named ‘Yogendar’ filed objections under Form-7 against 32 electors within the same Assembly Constituency in Hata, Kushinagar district.
claiming that “approximately 700-800 Form 7 objection applications seeking deletion of voters’ names were submitted in respect of Booth Nos. 71, 72, 73 and 74 of Assembly Constituency 313 Khalilabad

corrected_what_is_reported: Newslaundry reported from its investigation in Uttarakhand that numerous applications were filed to remove Muslim voters from the rolls, many in the names of people it said were associated with the BJP. It reported that some people named as objectors later filed affidavits saying they had never filed the objections and that their names, EPIC numbers and signatures had been used fraudulently.
evidence: A Newslaundry investigation into the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process in Uttarakhand has revealed a deeply concerning pattern.
Numerous applications were filed to remove the names of Muslim voters from the electoral rolls. Many of the individuals listed as applicants in these filings are associated with the BJP.

Some of the individuals in whose names these objections were filed later submitted affidavits stating that they had never filed them in the first place. They alleged that their names, EPIC numbers, and signatures had been fraudulently used.
problem: None in substance. The page is mainly a video, and its text is a short summary, so no figures can be checked against it.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Hindu reported that as of September 28, 4,000 Form 7 applications seeking deletion of names had been filed in Karnataka, which it said mostly targeted Muslim voters. It reported that ten people filed Form 7s seeking deletion of 1,363 names in Babaleshwar in one day, often on forms with the voters' details already printed and only the objector's name handwritten. Civil society groups and the Karnataka Congress demanded that the Commission lodge criminal complaints.
corrected_figures: 4,000 Form-7 applications as of September 28; 1,363 names in Babaleshwar by ten people in one day; in Bhalki 30 people filed Form-7s seeking deletion of 1,700 names
official_response: V. Anbukumar, CEO, Karnataka, was not available for comment.
evidence: Civil society groups and the Karnataka Congress have demanded that the Election Commission of India (ECI) lodge criminal complaints over bulk Form-7 applications ... allegedly targeting predominantly Muslim voters.
As of September 28, 4,000 Form-7 applications were filed in the State, mostly targeting Muslim voters in constituencies represented by both Congress and BJP.

Ten people filed Form-7s seeking deletion of 1,363 names in Babaleshwar in just one day. In many cases, the Form-7s submitted had details of the voters “already printed”, with only the objector’s name handwritten.
Mr. Khandre, who represents the Bhalki Assembly constituency where 30 people filed Form-7s seeking deletion of 1,700 names
V. Anbukumar, CEO, Karnataka, was not available for comment.
problem: None in substance. The item left out that the Karnataka CEO was not available for comment. Note that The Hindu states the Muslim-targeting finding in its own voice in the body, and as an allegation in the standfirst.

corrected_what_is_reported: The New Indian Express reported that the Commission wrote to election officials in Bengaluru that bulk Form 7 applications had come to its notice, with allegations that some were not genuine. It reported that the Commission directed Electoral Registration Officers to act against applicants who knowingly make false declarations, after an inquiry under Rule 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
official_response: The report is itself of a Commission letter: “Instances of bulk Form 7 applications had come to its notice and that allegations had been made that some of these applications were not genuine. It is directed the concerned EROs to initiate action against applicants who knowingly make false statements or declarations in writing while submitting Forms 6, 6A, 7 or 8.”
evidence: In a letter to District Election Officers, Additional District Election Officers, Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and senior civic officials in Bengaluru, the ECI specifically flagged reports of bulk applications being filed in Form 7

The Commission said, “Instances of bulk Form 7 applications had come to its notice and that allegations had been made that some of these applications were not genuine. It is directed the concerned EROs to initiate action against applicants who knowingly make false statements or declarations in writing while submitting Forms 6, 6A, 7 or 8.”
The ECI, however, made clear that any such action must be preceded by an inquiry under Rule 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that the online Form 6 on the Commission's ECINET portal carried a new declaration asking whether the applicant or their parents or grandparents were in the electoral roll of the last SIR, although the statutory form had not been amended. It reported that the section was not marked mandatory but applicants could not proceed to submission without completing it, and that the downloadable Form 6 on the same portal did not include it.
corrected_figures: over 5.58 crore names deleted in 10 states and three UTs; visible for all states and UTs where SIR concluded in 2025-2026 or is ongoing, except Bihar and Assam
official_response: The EC did not respond to a request for comment and Legislative Department Secretary Rajiv Mani could not be reached despite repeated attempts.
evidence: For the first time, the Election Commission’s online version of the electors’ registration form, known as Form 6, has a new section that seeks the status of the applicant’s parents vis-a vis the last Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, even though the statutory form itself has not been amended, The Indian Express has learnt.
But the copy of the Form 6 available for download on the same portal, ostensibly for filling and submitting physically, does not include this new declaration part.
This part of the form was visible for applicants from all states and UTs where the SIR has concluded in 2025-2026 or is currently ongoing, except for Bihar ... and Assam
While the new part has not been marked mandatory, the user cannot move forward toward the submission before completing it.
This comes when over 5.58 crore names have been deleted from electoral rolls in 10 states and three UTs
The EC did not respond to a request for comment and Legislative Department Secretary Rajiv Mani could not be reached despite repeated attempts.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported, from internal records it investigated, that on May 16 Election Commissioner Vivek Joshi recorded that Form 6 is prescribed by statute and cannot be altered without amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and that Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu concurred on May 19. It reported that the declaration was added to the online form anyway, and that on August 13 Sandhu wrote that the changes were unauthorised and illegal and must be removed immediately.
corrected_figures: Joshi note May 16; Sandhu concurred May 19; first reported July 12; Sandhu note August 13
evidence: On May 16, responding to the proposal to change Form 6 through the SIR framework, Election Commissioner Vivek Joshi recorded his objections.
Form 6 and Form 8 ...: they are “prescribed statutorily” and “cannot be altered without making amendments in the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960”.
On May 19, his colleague on the panel Sukhbir Singh Sandhu concurred with Joshi on file.

“In spite of these very clear views expressed by two Election Commissioners,” Sandhu wrote, the “unauthorised/ illegal changes in Form-6 on the portal” had not been removed and the original form had not been restored. The changes “must be removed immediately so that young and would-be first time voters, who are otherwise eligible, can register themselves as voters as per law, without any harassment”, he wrote.
problem: None. This article itself carries no Commission response. The Commission's general response to the series is given under items 21 and 22.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that on the night of 29 to 30 September 2026 the Commission removed the SIR declaration from the online Form 6 on ECINET for states where the final SIR rolls have been published. It reported that the declaration remained for states where the SIR is still ongoing.
official_response: The article cites the Commission's September 26 announcement that ‘for non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used’.
evidence: Four days after announcing the decision, the Election Commission, on the intervening night of Tuesday and Wednesday, removed the Special Intensive Revision declaration added to the statutory voter enrolment form, Form 6, from its ECINET application portal in states where the SIR has concluded.

On Wednesday night, the ECINET portal no longer showed the declaration – which had been inserted in between Sections J and K of the Form 6 online – for the states where the final SIR electoral rolls have been published so far. The declaration was still there for those states where the SIR is still ongoing.
The EC had on September 26 announced that ‘for non-SIR period, the Forms applicable as per Rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used’.
problem: None in the item. Note the article itself is internally inconsistent on timing. It says "the intervening night of Tuesday and Wednesday" and also "On Wednesday night", and it went live early on Wednesday 30 September. The item's "night of 29 to 30 September" follows the first phrasing.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that Kanchan Kumar Mondal, 75, died of cardiac arrest, according to hospital sources, after falling ill in a queue for an SIR hearing at the Rampurhat-1 block office in Birbhum. His wife and family alleged the SIR process had caused him excessive stress and held the Election Commission responsible. It also reported that Madan Ghosh died of cardiac arrest at an SIR hearing in Howrah the previous day.
corrected_figures: aged 75
evidence: A 75-year-old man died due to cardiac arrest while attending a hearing related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process in Birbhum district on Saturday morning.
The deceased, identified as Kanchan Kumar Mondal, had received a notice for an SIR hearing and accordingly appeared at the Rampurhat-1 Block Office along with his wife.

According to hospital sources, Mondal died due to cardiac arrest. However, his wife and family alleged that he had fallen ill due to excessive stress related to the SIR process, and they held the Election Commission responsible for his death.
A similar incident occurred in Howrah on Friday. An elderly man, Madan Ghosh, died due to cardiac arrest while attending a SIR-related hearing at the Bally Jagacha Block Office in Domjur.

corrected_what_is_reported: The New Indian Express, citing PTI, reported that police in Purulia registered an FIR on a complaint by the son of Durjan Majhi, 82, who died allegedly by suicide on 29 December hours before he was due at an SIR hearing. An officer was quoted as saying the case included charges of abetment of suicide and criminal conspiracy against Election Commission officials, with no official named. The family alleged he acted out of anxiety over the SIR.
corrected_figures: aged 82; Trinamool Congress claimed at least 40 deaths since November 2025
evidence: According to the report citing officials, the FIR was registered based on the complaint of the deceased's son.

"The case includes charges of abetment of suicide and criminal conspiracy against officials of the Election Commission. No official was named in the FIR," an officer was quoted as saying by the news agency.
Durjan Majhi, a tribal man of Choutala village in Para block, died allegedly by suicide on December 29, hours before he was scheduled to appear for an SIR hearing.
Majhi's family alleged that he ended his life due to anxiety over the SIR.

According to the ruling Trinamool Congress, at least 40 people, including Booth Level Officers (BLO) have died allegedly due to workload, stress and anxiety related to the SIR, since the exercise began in November 2025.

corrected_what_is_reported: India Today reported from Hajipur and Muzaffarpur that BLOs were accepting and submitting enumeration forms without supporting documents at their own discretion. It reported that BLOs admitted the practice varied by location, with some accepting Aadhaar and others not.
evidence: In Bihar’s ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, Booth Level Officers (BLOs) are now accepting and submitting voter enumeration forms without any supporting documents, solely based on their discretion.
A ground investigation by India Today in Hajipur and Muzaffarpur has revealed that document submission has become flexible, and in some cases, optional.
BLOs admitted that discretion is being exercised differently across locations. Some accept Aadhaar, others do not.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Hindu reported that married women in Bihar born after 1 July 1987 were struggling in the SIR because they needed documents from their parental homes rather than their marital homes. It quoted women in Araria and Katihar districts who said their parents had no documents to give, and a woman in Saharsa, born in 1965, whose parents had died and who did not know what documents she needed.
evidence: Married women born between July 1, 1987 to December 2, 2004 and born after December 2, 2004 are at the receiving end in the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) as they need to provide the documents related to the maternal house (Maika) instead of in-laws (Sasural).
Munni Devi of Araria district ... “I contacted my mother Lalvati Devi and father Bindeshwari Rishidev for the document, they said they themselves have no document to submit.”
She asserted that her mother Savti Devi and father Bishan Mandal have no documents to submit

Sumitra Devi born in 1965 is a worried woman as her father and mother’s parents have passed more than decades ago. She is the voter of Sonbharasa assembly constituency and resident of Lalpur village under Banma Itahri block in Saharsa district.
Ms. Sumitra said she has no idea what kind of document she requires of her deceased parents.
problem: The item said the women quoted in Araria, Katihar and Saharsa all said their parents had no documents. The Saharsa woman, Sumitra Devi, was born in 1965, outside the post-1987 group the article is about, and her complaint was that her parents had died and she did not know what documents were needed. Published 25 July 2025 at 10:27 pm IST, updated 26 July.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Telegraph reported that migrant workers from Samserganj in Murshidabad were served SIR hearing notices two to three days before their hearings and had to travel home from Uttar Pradesh and Kerala without reserved seats. One worker was summoned because his name appeared in the 2002 roll without a surname, and another arrived after the day's hearings had ended. It reported that, as of 1 January, the Commission had issued no directive allowing online hearings for those outside the state.
corrected_figures: about 1,400 km from Meerut; nearly 2,600 km from Kollam; a loss of about Rs 15,000 for one worker
official_response: Samserganj BDO Sujit Kumar Lodh: “After receiving the notice, those who are unable to attend the hearing within the stipulated period because of being out of the house can submit a written application citing specific reasons, and a second hearing date will be scheduled for them later.”
evidence: The notice had been issued the same day, leaving him barely three days to reach his home, almost 1,400km away from Meerut in Uttar Pradesh.
The reason behind his ordeal was an entry made over two decades ago, when his name appeared in the 2002 electoral roll simply as “Samed”, without his surname
Rahim learnt about it over the phone, with less than 48 hours to make the journey back, which entails covering a distance of nearly 2,600km.
he finally reached home late on December 30, nearly 10 hours after the day’s hearings had concluded.
Altogether, this has caused a loss of about ₹15,000.
However, till Thursday, the Election Commission had issued no directive allowing online hearings for those staying outside the state

However, with notices in many cases being served barely 48 hours before the scheduled hearing, migrant workers find themselves scrambling to return home in time, often without seats and at a high financial cost.

corrected_what_is_reported: The BBC reported that voters in villages near Patna told it the Bihar draft roll carried wrong photographs, duplicate entries and the name of a person who died more than five years earlier. It reported that in Danara village many residents were not sure officials had visited their homes.
corrected_figures: 72.4 million names on the draft roll, 6.5 million fewer than before; the Commission says deletions include 2.2 million dead, 700,000 enrolled more than once and 3.6 million migrated
official_response: In response to the BBC's questions, the Election Commission shared its 24 June order on conducting the SIR and a 27 July press note outlining efforts to ensure no eligible voter was "left behind". "Further, [the commission] does not take any responsibility of any other misinformation or unsubstantiated allegations being floated around by some vested interests," it added. The BBC also noted the commission has said BLOs worked "very responsibly".
evidence: many voters in Bihar have told the BBC that the draft rolls have wrong photos and include dead people.
He shared pages showing his family's details - pointing out errors, including the wrong photo next to his name.
He points out the name of a cousin who died more than five years back but still figures on the list - and at least two names that appear twice.
Most residents had little to no idea about SIR or its impact, and many weren't sure if officials had even visited their homes.
The new draft rolls have 72.4 million names - 6.5 million fewer than before.
The poll body and BJP have denied the allegations. In response to the BBC's questions, the Election Commission shared its 24 June order on conducting the SIR and a 27 July press note

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi warned on file, from November 2025 to August 2026, that control of the electoral roll software was being centralised in the Commission's IT division. It reported that on August 14 Sandhu wrote that many Chief Electoral Officers, District Election Officers and Electoral Registration Officers had told him they lacked proper and complete access to ERONet, and that on July 29 both Commissioners wrote separately to the Cabinet Secretary about a change in work allocation.
corrected_figures: letters by Deputy Election Commissioner Sanjay Kumar dated November 4, 2025 (on Sandhu's directions) and January 2, 2026; Sandhu note April 16; Joshi note May 29; Sandhu endorsement July 13; letters to the Cabinet Secretary July 29; joint note July 30; Sandhu note August 14
official_response: The Election Commission and the two ECs, Sandhu and Joshi, did not respond to calls and questionnaires emailed by The Indian Express seeking comment.
evidence: Over ten months, from November to August, the two Commissioners said so repeatedly and in writing
On November 4, 2025, acting on Sandhu’s directions, Deputy Election Commissioner Sanjay Kumar wrote to Khanna and senior Commission officers
January 2, 2026: ... Sanjay Kumar wrote to Khanna, asking her to “ensure that IT system is made in a manner that ERO’s discretion to act in any manner is not restricted”.
July 29: In a move without precedent, the two Commissioners each wrote separately to the Cabinet Secretary reporting the above order

But many had told him they did not have “proper and complete access” to ERONet and were therefore unable to perform their statutory duties properly. Their powers, he said, had been “curtailed by centralised control of ERONet at DG(IT) level”.
The Election Commission and the two ECs, Sandhu and Joshi, did not respond to calls and questionnaires emailed by The Indian Express seeking comment.
problem: The figures listed November 4, 2025 and January 2, 2026 as notes by the Commissioners. Both were written by Deputy Election Commissioner Sanjay Kumar, the first on Sandhu's directions. The other dates were also missing the July 30 joint note and listed July 28, which was the date of the Garg order, not a Commissioner note.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that Goa's Electoral Registration Officers heard electors flagged for logical discrepancies and found 97 of them eligible, but could not reverse the earlier decisions on ECINET because the permission was controlled from Delhi. It reported that the Goa Chief Electoral Officer's office wrote eight times in seven days asking for a rollback option, and that all 97 were missing from the final roll published on February 21 and were still missing on September 20.
corrected_figures: 649 electors came forward with documents or objections; 97 found eligible; eight emails in seven days (February 11 to 17); 65 of the 97 from Taleigao
official_response: Goa Chief Electoral Officer Sanjay Goel: “We apprised the ECI about the cases to be included wherein voters were flagged for logical discrepancies.” ... “The call (to not include) was theirs. But there has to be some mechanism (in ECINET) to re-include voters at the ERO level.” DG (IT) Seema Khanna did not respond to a questionnaire. The Indian Express reported on 2026-09-27 that, in the note issued after its meeting of September 26, the Commission says 81 of the 97 have now filled Form 6 and the CEO has been directed to facilitate their inclusion (https://indianexpress.com/article/explained/election-commission-nine-new-decisions-what-changes-and-what-doesnt-10895475/).
evidence: Attached was a list of 97 voters whom Goa’s own Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) had heard, examined and found eligible
But the EROs could not reverse those decisions through the software (ECINet). Reason: the permission to do so was controlled from Delhi.
On February 17, four days before Goa was due to publish its final electoral roll ... the state’s Chief Electoral Officer wrote to the ECI in Delhi. This was his eighth time in seven days.
On February 21, the final roll was published. The Indian Express checked all 97 names against it. Until September 20, all 97 are still missing.
According to the CEO’s emails, 649 electors came forward with documents or objections.
The Indian Express sent a questionnaire to Seema Khanna ... There was no response.

In Goa, where The Indian Express found 97 voters cleared by local officers still missing from the final roll, the Commission says 81 have now filled Form 6 and the CEO has been directed to facilitate their inclusion. (Indian Express, 27 September 2026)

corrected_what_is_reported: The Hindu reported that 13 days into the Karnataka SIR only 0.41% of enumeration forms had been submitted online, and that voters complained of captcha failures, server errors and an ECINet search that failed to find records appearing in the published rolls. It reported that online submission required a current mobile number linked to the voter's EPIC.
corrected_figures: 0.41% submitted online as of 6 pm on July 12; up 0.23% between July 5 and July 12
official_response: Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer V. Anbu Kumar said the process was still under way. However, the CEO did not comment on the technical glitches reported by voters.
evidence: Even 13 days after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began across Karnataka, not even 0.5% of voters have submitted their enumeration forms online.
As of 6 p.m. on Sunday, only 0.41% of the forms were submitted online. Captcha failures, slow browser response and repeated errors have been reported by those attempting to fill the forms online.
In the past one week between July 5 and July 12, online submissions jumped only by 0.23%.
online forms can only be submitted if the voter’s current mobile number is linked to their Elector Photo Identity Card (EPIC).
Several citizens also reported that while their names and details appear correctly in the publicly available PDF electoral rolls, the ECINet search portal fails to retrieve their records
Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) V. Anbu Kumar said the process was still under way. However, the CEO did not comment on the technical glitches reported by voters.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally objected on record at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders that, they say, were taken without their knowledge. It reported that the objections concerned new voter registration, deletion and restoration of voters, appeals against orders restoring voters, and the custody and security of the electoral roll, and said it had seen each of these exchanges.
corrected_figures: at least 14 times over the last 10 months; four times on a single day; more than 13 crore names struck off the draft rolls in 30 States and Union Territories
official_response: The Indian Express wrote that it sent a questionnaire to the Commission on September 21 and emailed both Commissioners, and "There was no response." The Hindu reported on 2026-09-23 that the ECI first issued a source-based clarification: "All decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR [the ongoing special intensive revision of electoral rolls], have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner." A formal written statement followed: "The Commission operates as a multi-member constitutional body. Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour. All actions of ECI have been in accordance of laws and instructions of the Commission." (https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/differing-views-observations-are-normal-part-of-deliberation-in-any-institution-eci-on-reports-of-internal-friction/article71499104.ece)
evidence: But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months – four times on a single day – to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge.

For, the objections relate to the core of the Election Commission’s mandate: new voter registration, deletion and restoration of voters in the rolls; filing of appeals against orders restoring voters in the SIR process; and the custody, and security, of the entire electoral roll itself.
The Indian Express has seen each of these exchanges
has struck more than 13 crore names off the draft voter rolls in 30 States and Union Territories.
On September 21, The Indian Express sent a questionnaire to the Commission ... There was no response.

The ECI first issued a source-based clarification to the report. “All decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR ..., have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner,” the clarification said. (The Hindu)
A formal, written statement followed. “... All actions of ECI have been in accordance of laws and instructions of the Commission,” it said. (The Hindu)
problem: The quoted 'unanimous' line was presented as the Commission's statement. The Hindu describes it as a source-based clarification, and the Commission's formal written statement that followed was omitted. The Hindu article is dated 23 September 2026, as the item says. The summary and quote themselves are accurate.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Indian Express reported that in August Election Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu wrote to Commission officials asking who had authorised and who had filed appeals on behalf of the Commission against voters whom judicial officers had included in West Bengal. It reported that he recorded that neither he, nor Commissioner Vivek Joshi, nor the current Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal had been informed of the basis or process of filing those appeals.
corrected_figures: 38 lakh appeals pending before the tribunals, as the Commission told the court; 22.21 lakh filed by deleted voters seeking to be restored; 16.10 lakh filed against voters the judicial officers had included
official_response: The Indian Express wrote that it sent a questionnaire to the Commission on September 21 and emailed both Commissioners, and "There was no response." The Hindu reported on 2026-09-23 that the ECI first issued a source-based clarification: "All decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR [the ongoing special intensive revision of electoral rolls], have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner." A formal written statement followed: "The Commission operates as a multi-member constitutional body. Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks-and-balances are standard, ongoing practices designed to ensure complete transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour. All actions of ECI have been in accordance of laws and instructions of the Commission." (https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/differing-views-observations-are-normal-part-of-deliberation-in-any-institution-eci-on-reports-of-internal-friction/article71499104.ece)
evidence: In August, he wrote to Commission officials asking, “Who was authorised to file these appeals on behalf of ECI, and by whom?” and “Who actually filed these appeals on behalf of ECI?” He recorded that neither he nor Joshi nor the current Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal had been informed about the basis or process of filing the appeals.

Last week, the Commission told the court that there were 38 lakh appeals pending before the tribunals: 22.21 lakh filed by deleted voters seeking to be restored. The other 16.10 lakh were filed against voters the judicial officers had included, seeking their deletion. The Commission did not say who filed those.
problem: Official response was null although the same article records the Commission's non-response, and the Commission's later statement applies to the whole series. On items 21 and 22: they share one URL and headline, but they are distinct claims from one article. Item 21 is the article's headline finding (14 objections in 10 months). Item 22 is its separate West Bengal section on who filed the appeals. It is not a duplicate entry, but the page should show both as drawn from the same article so readers do not count them as two independent reports.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Wire reported that Mintu Paswan of Ara, Bhojpur, who had been declared dead in the Bihar draft roll, appeared alive in the Supreme Court on 12 August 2025, produced by petitioner Yogendra Yadav. Paswan told The Wire he had filled the enumeration form and that the BLO came to his house only after he complained.
corrected_figures: aged 41; 65 lakh left out of the draft roll of August 1; 22 lakh declared deceased, 36 lakh permanently shifted or not found, seven lakh duplicated
official_response: Senior advocate Rakesh Dwivedi, for the Commission, called the production of Paswan "drama". The bench of Justices Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi said there may have been an "inadvertent error", which could be rectified.
evidence: Forty-one-year-old Mintu Paswan, a resident of Bihar’s Ara assembly constituency in Bhojpur district was declared dead by the Election Commission in its ongoing ‘special intensive revision’ of the electoral rolls in the poll-bound state. But on August 12, Paswan appeared in the Supreme Court, demonstrably alive.
Paswan was one of two people produced in court by psephologist and activist Yogendra Yadav
Paswan, who works as a driver in Ara, said to The Wire that he had filled the enumeration form and yet his name was struck off.
Paswan said that it was only after he lodged a complaint that the Booth Level Officer (BLO) visited his house.
of the 65 lakhs who have been excluded, 22 lakh voters were declared deceased

The move to produce Paswan in court was referred to as “drama” by senior advocate Rakesh Dwivedi who was appearing for the Election Commission. ... The bench of Justices Surya Kant and Joymalya Bagchi however said there may have been an “inadvertent error”, which could be rectified.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Reporters' Collective reported, from internal Commission records it acquired, that the Commission's software initially flagged 1.31 crore voters in West Bengal and 2.35 crore in Madhya Pradesh for logical discrepancies, and that officials had no written instructions on how to resolve them. It reported that no criteria for deciding which flagged voters to summon had been made public.
corrected_figures: 1.31 crore (17.11%) in West Bengal; 2.35 crore in Madhya Pradesh (given as both 41.22% and nearly 40%); West Bengal count fell to 95 lakh by January 2, per The Hindu citing sources; 24 lakh of 95 lakh to receive notices, per a Commission leak to the press
official_response: We asked ECI about the criterion used, but they did not reply at the time of filing the report. The Collective also wrote that questions on testing of the digitisation, and on the SOP, sent to the ECI and three state CEO offices went unanswered.
evidence: The untested software deployed by the Election Commission of India (ECI) without written instructions, protocols and manuals, red-flagged 1.31 crore voters in West Bengal and 2.35 crore voters in Madhya Pradesh as suspicious, putting their voting rights in jeopardy.
These voters earmarked as suspicious comprised a whopping 17.11% of the voting population in West Bengal and 41.22% of the voting population in Madhya Pradesh.
The Collective acquired a few of the ECI’s internal records ... In Madhya Pradesh, nearly 40% of the voters on the draft roll (2.35 crore voters) were deemed ‘suspect’
By January 2, this number had dropped to 95 lakh, The Hindu reported, citing sources in the state chief electoral officer’s office.

In the case of West Bengal, 24 lakh of the 95 lakh flagged will receive notices of summons, the Commission leaked to the press. No public disclosures on the criteria used to summon voters or resolve discrepancies have been made. We asked ECI about the criterion used, but they did not reply at the time of filing the report.
problem: None in substance. The article gives two figures for the Madhya Pradesh share (41.22% and nearly 40%), so the page should not state a single percentage as exact.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Reporters' Collective reported that hearing notices in West Bengal were generated in bulk by the Commission's software for logical discrepancies, and that two EROs it spoke to, with a few deputies, were signing 4,000 to 5,000 printed notices each day. It reported that the software transliterated names from Bengali into English before matching, so that spellings such as Xalxo and Khalkho triggered a discrepancy. The Collective said this showed the Commission had misled the Supreme Court, where it said there was no automated generation of notices.
corrected_figures: over 1.5 crore summons prepared; 95.39 lakh delivered and 30 lakh attended by January 24; software marked more than 1.31 crore voters; over 32 lakh unmapped in the draft of December 16
official_response: We sent questions to the ECI to respond to the story. It had not responded by the time of publication. The Commission's submission to the Court, as quoted: “There is no automated generation of notices…. EROs (Electoral Registration Officers) are signing them off after application of mind.”
evidence: We found that the ECI had misled the Supreme Court. It told the court, “There is no automated generation of notices…. EROs (Electoral Registration Officers) are signing them off after application of mind.”
Our investigation shows, contrary to the ECI’s claim before the Supreme Court, the notices in West Bengal have been generated en masse by centralised and untested algorithms
We spoke to two EROs, one in Kolkata and one in Nadia, who, along with a few deputies, were signing 4,000 to 5,000 printed hearing notices each day.

The primary issue, as a senior official explained, is that the software translates voter rolls from Bengali into English before attempting a match. In numerous instances, the traditional English spelling of a surname differs from the software's automated transliteration of the Bengali script.
While over 1.5 crore summons were prepared, officials have delivered only 95.39 lakh, with just 30 lakh voters attending proceedings by January 24.
According to West Bengal’s draft voter lists published on December 16, over 32 lakh voters in West Bengal were unmapped.
We sent questions to the ECI to respond to the story. It had not responded by the time of publication.
problem: The sentence "This contrasts with the Commission's submission to the Supreme Court" stated the contradiction in the page's own voice. It is The Reporters' Collective's finding, made in its headline ("ECI misled the Supreme Court"), and must be attributed to it. The item also said "EROs it interviewed" were signing the notices. The Collective interviewed five EROs, and the 4,000 to 5,000 a day figure comes from two of them, working with deputies.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Hindu reported that up to 11 categories of logical discrepancy were being applied in the third phase of the SIR, up from four when the concept was introduced in West Bengal. They include a sibling age gap of nine months or less, which flagged a Delhi resident's twin children, and a marital mapping mismatch where a woman is linked to her father in the old roll and her husband in the new. It reported that the term has never been clearly defined in any official communication.
corrected_figures: about 1.36 crore notices in West Bengal; 19.33 lakh in Delhi; 20.35 lakh in Karnataka; up to 11 categories against original four
evidence: Up to 11 distinct categories of logical discrepancies have been identified and applied across various States and Union Territories ... expanding from the original four categories initially used when the concept was introduced during West Bengal’s SIR exercise.
he learnt that his children had been flagged despite being in the draft list as the age gap between them was not more than nine months. Well, it cannot be since his 30-year-old children are twins.
marital mapping mismatch (e.g., female voter linked to her father in the previous roll but mapped to her husband in the current roll without cross-referencing)

The logical discrepancy category first surfaced during the SIR in West Bengal when approximately 1.36 crore voters received notices. In Delhi, where SIR is being done currently, 19.33 lakh electors have received discrepancy notices while 20.35 lakh have received the notices in Karnataka.

The problem in this is that “logical discrepancies” has never been clearly defined in any official communication — neither in the Election Commission’s notice in May 2026 nor in the original SIR order from June 2025.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Reporters' Collective reported that a top Commission official and four Bihar EROs confirmed to it that the Commission did not run its de-duplication software during the Bihar SIR and did not give state officials access to it. It quoted the official saying the focus was on document collection. It reported that its own earlier analysis of the final roll found 14.35 lakh suspect duplicate entries.
corrected_figures: 14.35 lakh suspect duplicate entries in the final roll, 3.4 lakh exact matches on name, relative's name and age; 5.56 lakh suspect duplicates in the draft in 142 constituencies
official_response: We emailed questions to the ECI and its top official in Bihar, the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO). Neither of them replied to us. In person, Bihar CEO Vinod Singh Gunjiyal told the reporter, on whether the de-duplication software was accessible in Bihar: “We cannot share this information with you.” On whether the ECI had sent a list of duplicates: “There is a legal procedure in place for any such process—the Supreme Court is hearing the entire matter, and we are presenting everything there, and you can leave.” The Collective also records that the CEO had earlier said on social media that the draft was only a draft and errors would be removed before finalising.
evidence: This was confirmed to The Reporters’ Collective by a top official of the Election Commission of India (ECI) in Delhi and four Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) in Bihar.
They confirmed that ECI had neither given state officials access to the software to detect frauds and duplicates on their own, nor had ECI carried out this exercise at the central database level
A top official at ECI who spoke with us said, “We did not touch deduplication during SIR. Mostly our focus was on document collection.”

Our previous report revealed that the final Bihar voter roll for all 243 assembly constituencies now holds 14.35 lakh suspect duplicate entries. Of these, 3.4 lakh entries are exact matches on all three demographic parameters
In the draft list, we found 5.56 lakh suspect duplicates in 142 assembly constituencies.
We emailed questions to the ECI and its top official in Bihar, the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO). Neither of them replied to us.
To which he replied, “We cannot share this information with you.”
He replied, “There is a legal procedure in place for any such process—the Supreme Court is hearing the entire matter, and we are presenting everything there, and you can leave.”
The CEO of Bihar said that it was only a draft voter list and any errors would be removed before finalising it.
problem: The official response gave only the email non-response. The article also records the Bihar CEO's in-person replies and his earlier public statement that draft-roll errors would be removed before finalisation, which were omitted. The 14.35 lakh figure comes from the Collective's previous report, cited in this article, not from new analysis in this piece.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Wire reported that tribunal orders in Murshidabad record the Additional Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal as the appellant against electors whom judicial officers had restored to the roll. It reported that appeal records it reviewed carry identical minute-level timestamps across different constituencies, including at least six appeals at 7.04 pm on 8 April 2026, which it reads as indicating a centralised script rather than individual filings. It also reported a December 2025 letter from the WBCS (Executive) Officers' Association complaining of system-driven deletions that bypassed EROs.
corrected_figures: 38,31,429 appeals filed; 22,21,118 from excluded voters; 16,10,311 against inclusion; 32,77,360 electors cleared by judicial officers (figures from the Commission's September 16 reply in the Supreme Court)
official_response: The ECI has not yet clarified why more than 16 lakh challenges were filed by the commission, how the electors were selected and what explains the batch pattern visible in the appeal records.
evidence: The second line of the order reads, “This is an appeal filed by the Additional CEO as regards” the elector, who is then named in full.
Screenshots from the Election Commission’s appeal portal reviewed by The Wire show at least six such appeals carrying the exact timestamp 08/04/2026 | 19:04.
The uniform execution across divergent geographical jurisdictions indicates a centralised script running over an electoral list rather than individual filings by field officers.

On December 24, 2025, ... the WBCS (Executive) Officers’ Association wrote to the Chief Electoral Officer of West Bengal. The subject line of their email reads, “Suo-motu system-driven deletion of electors from the draft electoral rolls in West Bengal in the ongoing SIR process bypassing the statutory role of the EROs.”
Of 38,31,429 (roughly 38 lakh) appeals filed, 22,21,118 (22 lakh) came from voters whose names had been excluded or deleted. And 16,10,311 (16 lakh plus) were appeals against inclusion.
Set against the 32,77,360 (roughly 32 lakh) electors, the judicial officers examined and cleared
The ECI has not yet clarified why more than 16 lakh challenges were filed by the commission, how the electors were selected and what explains the batch pattern visible in the appeal records.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Telegraph reported that Justice (retd) Indrajit Chatterjee, who presides over one of the 19 SIR appellate tribunals and hears appeals from 11 Murshidabad constituencies, has written to the Chief Justice of Calcutta High Court that he wants to resign, citing a long commute. He told the newspaper he can decide about 10 appeals a day and has decided 425, restoring 350, while around 5.3 lakh are pending before him. It also reported that two other tribunal judges had resigned earlier, citing personal reasons.
corrected_figures: Appeals disposed of: 425; restored 350, struck off 75; appeals pending: around 5.3 lakh; about 10 appeals a day; around 145 years at that rate; 82.35 per cent genuine voters; over 38 lakh appeals filed, over 37 lakh pending, about 1.02 lakh disposed of (per the Commission's affidavit)
official_response: An official of the state election commission: “The tribunals were set up on the Supreme Court’s order. A panel headed by the chief justice of Calcutta High Court takes decisions regarding the functioning of the appellate tribunals. We cannot interfere.”
evidence: Appeals disposed of: 425. Appeals pending: Around 5.3 lakh.

Justice (retd) Indrajit Chatterjee, who presides over one of the 19 appellate tribunals ... has written to the chief justice of Calcutta High Court, saying he wanted to resign from the tribunal. He has cited a long daily commute
For as long as he has worked, he could only hear about 10 appeals a day. At this rate, it will take around 145 years to dispose of all the remaining 5 lakh cases if he works 365 days a year.
“I have decided 425 appeals so far. The names of 350 appellants have been restored to the rolls and 75 have been struck off,” Justice Chatterjee told The Telegraph on Wednesday.
He decides appeals from 11 constituencies.
In May, former chief justice of Calcutta High Court, Justice T.S. Sivagnanam, stepped down citing personal reasons. In July, Justice Ranjit Bag also resigned citing personal reasons.
According to the affidavit, over 37 lakh appeals remain pending, with only about 1.02 lakh cases disposed of.

corrected_what_is_reported: The Hans India reported that Andhra Pradesh's Chief Electoral Officer announced a door-to-door re-check of 46,62,583 names before the final roll of 16 October. They are the 44,89,512 left off the draft and the 1,73,071 found ineligible after notices, and booth officers are to help anyone left off in error file Form 6.
corrected_figures: 46,62,583 names on the lists; 44,89,512 electors not available at their registered addresses at enumeration; 1,73,071 found ineligible as on 6 October; draft roll of 31 July 3,71,38,182 electors
official_response: The paper quoted the Chief Electoral Officer, Vivek Yadav, as saying the drive will recheck the flagged cases, and that a name found deleted by mistake is to be restored through Form 6 after verification.
evidence: Chief Electoral Officer and E O Vivek Yadav said Booth Level Officers (BLOs) would begin fresh door-to-door verification from Thursday, carrying polling-station-wise lists of 46,62,583 deleted names.

During the enumeration phase from June 15 to July 24, BLOs conducted house-to-house verification and found 44,89,512 electors not available at their registered addresses due to death, permanent migration, multiple enrolments, untraceability and other reasons.
During the subsequent notice phase, another 1,73,071 electors were found ineligible as on October 6 for inclusion in the final roll.
If an elector is found to have been deleted inadvertently, the BLOs will facilitate filing of Form-6, enabling restoration of the name after due verification through continuous updation.
problem: The 46,62,583 are not all deleted names. 44,89,512 were left off the draft and 1,73,071 were found ineligible after notices, for exclusion from the final roll. The same drive is behind the Deccan Chronicle report already cited for 1,73,071 in notices.csv.
